Au Sénégal, améliorer la production locale de riz ne dépend pas seulement de la disponibilité de semences performantes. Pour les petits producteurs, l’accès au crédit et la sécurité des droits fonciers peuvent aussi déterminer la capacité à adopter des variétés améliorées.

En tant que chercheurs, nous étudions l’économie appliquée et le développement agricole, notamment les liens entre financement, sécurité foncière et adoption des innovations par les producteurs.

Notre récente étude montre que le crédit ne favorise pas systématiquement l'adoption des variétés améliorées. Ses effets varient selon que les agriculteurs disposent ou non de droits fonciers sécurisés. Ce constat souligne l’importance de penser ensemble financement agricole et réforme foncière.

La sécurité foncière désigne la stabilité et la garantie des droits d’usage de la terre. Elle renforce la confiance des producteurs dans les investissements agricoles à long terme.

À l’inverse, l’insécurité foncière se caractérise par la précarité des droits sur les parcelles, notamment dans le cadre des régimes fonciers coutumiers, et peut décourager les investissements durables dans les exploitations.

Pertinence de l’étude

Dans notre étude , nous avons examiné le rôle de l’accès au crédit dans l’adoption de variétés de riz améliorées et certifiées au Sénégal, en mettant l’accent sur la manière dont la sécurité foncière conditionne cette relation.

Le riz représente près des deux tiers des importations céréalières du pays, et la production domestique reste limitée par la prédominance de petites exploitations (souvent inférieures à un hectare), l’accès restreint au crédit et l’insécurité foncière.

Read more: Gel de l'aide américaine : une menace potentielle pour l’agriculture au Sénégal

Nous utilisons des données secondaires issues de l’Enquête agricole annuelle 2021/2022 réalisée par la Direction de l’analyse, de la prévision et des statistiques agricoles (DAPSA) du ministère de l'Agriculture. L’échantillon retenu porte spécifiquement sur la production de riz et comprend 644 ménages agricoles.

Les variables clés incluent l’accès au crédit, la sécurité foncière (présence ou non d’un titre formel), la superficie cultivée, la taille du ménage, le niveau d’éducation, le statut matrimonial, l’accès aux subventions, ainsi que des caractéristiques démographiques.

La méthodologie repose sur un modèle à double seuil (double-hurdle). Celui-ci permet d’analyser l’adoption d’une innovation en deux étapes distinctes : d’abord, la décision du producteur de l’adopter ou non (la marge extensive) ; ensuite, le degré d’utilisation de cette innovation par les producteurs qui l’ont adoptée, mesuré ici par la proportion des terres consacrées aux variétés améliorées (la marge intensive).

Nous estimons le modèle sur l’ensemble de l’échantillon, puis séparément pour les ménages bénéficiant d’une tenure sécurisée et ceux dont la tenure ne l’est pas. Un ménage est considéré comme bénéficiant d’une tenure sécurisée lorsque le producteur dispose de droits fonciers stables, clairement définis et protégés à long terme sur sa parcelle.

Read more: Financement de l'agriculture : un modèle économique identifie la meilleure combinaison pour 10 pays africains

À l’inverse, un ménage est considéré comme étant en tenure non sécurisée lorsque ses droits d’accès à la terre sont précaires, informels ou contestables. Cette distinction permet de mettre en évidence les effets différenciés de l’accès au crédit selon le niveau de sécurité foncière. Des tests de diagnostic, notamment le test de Wald de séparabilité et les facteurs d’inflation de la variance (VIF), confortent le choix

Les principaux résultats montrent qu’en moyenne, sur l’ensemble de l’échantillon, sans distinction selon le niveau de sécurité foncière, l’accès au crédit n’a pas d’effet statistiquement significatif sur l’adoption des variétés améliorées. Il n’influence ni la décision des agriculteurs de les adopter ni la part des terres qu’ils leur consacrent. C’est en distinguant les ménages selon leur niveau de sécurité foncière que l’effet du crédit apparaît.

Ce résultat global masque toutefois des différences marquées selon le statut foncier. Chez les ménages bénéficiant d’une tenure sécurisée, l’accès au crédit est positivement et significativement associé tant à la décision d’adopter les variétés améliorées qu’à la part des terres qui leur est consacrée.

En revanche, chez les ménages en situation d’insécurité foncière, l’accès au crédit est négativement associé à la décision d’adopter des variétés améliorées, tandis que son effet sur la part des terres qui leur est consacrée n’est pas statistiquement significatif. Autrement dit, même si un agriculteur incertain de pouvoir conserver sa parcelle décide d’investir dans ces semences, il peut hésiter à leur consacrer une grande partie de ses terres.

Face au risque de perdre sa parcelle, l’agriculteur peut préférer consacrer une très petite superficie aux variétés améliorées afin de limiter ses pertes matérielles et financières. C’est ce que nous appelons un mécanisme de substitution sous contrainte.

Les tests de robustesse indiquent par ailleurs que ces associations conditionnelles résistent aux biais potentiellement liés aux variables non observées.

Read more: Dans les pays du Sud, la transition agroécologique au défi du financement

Le crédit ne suffit pas à favoriser l’adoption des variétés améliorées

L’absence d’effet moyen positif du crédit s’explique notamment par le rôle de la sécurité foncière. Dans le contexte sénégalais, de nombreux agriculteurs sont confrontés au rationnement du crédit : les banques et les institutions financières leur refusent des prêts ou leur accordent des montants inférieurs à leurs besoins. Environ 61 % des ménages seraient concernés, tandis que seule une faible proportion du crédit provient d’institutions financières formelles.

La terre ne peut souvent pas servir de garantie en raison de l’insécurité foncière, de la prévalence de droits coutumiers peu reconnus formellement, et des restrictions sur les transactions foncières.

Pour les ménages en tenure sécurisée, le crédit fonctionne comme un levier de liquidité : il permet de surmonter le coût initial d’acquisition des semences améliorées, dans un horizon d’investissement suffisamment long grâce à la possibilité de garantir la terre.

Ce résultat positif rejoint les conclusions d’autres études ont déjà prouvé : pour que le crédit fonctionne et soit efficace, il faut s'adresser à des agriculteurs qui ont des terres sécurisées ou du matériel, mais qui manquent simplement de financement pour démarrer la saison.

Chez les ménages dont la terre n'est pas sécurisée, trois mécanismes non exclusifs expliquent l’association négative.

Premièrement , une sélection et une réallocation : les prêteurs peuvent cibler ces ménages pour des besoins de liquidité de court terme (remboursement de dettes informelles, lissage de consommation) plutôt que pour l’investissement technologique ; le crédit reçu est alors détourné.

Deuxièmement , des arbitrages de choix de cultures sous contrainte foncière : sur des parcelles limitées ou faisant l'objet de litige, le coût d’opportunité d’allouer de la terre à des variétés améliorées (incertitude de rendement, investissement initial) est élevé ; le crédit peut faciliter le maintien d’un portefeuille de cultures traditionnelles moins risquées.

Troisièmement , quand un agriculteur n'est pas sûr de garder sa terre, le fait de s'endetter devient une stratégie à risque. S'il emprunte pour tester une nouvelle technique agricole et que la récolte ne soit pas rentable (ou qu'on lui prenne son champ), il se retrouve ruiné et accablé de dettes. Pour éviter cette situation, il préfère jouer la sécurité en refusant de changer ses vieilles habitudes.

Ces mécanismes entretiennent un cercle vicieux : l’insécurité foncière réduit la possibilité d’utiliser la terre comme garantie, ce qui limite l’accès au crédit formel et freine l’adoption des variétés améliorées. Le recours à des crédits informels coûteux peut alors accentuer ces difficultés.

En somme, le crédit n’est pas un instrument neutre ni systématiquement favorable à l’adoption : son effet dépend de la possibilité d’utiliser la terre comme garantie et de la sécurité des droits fonciers, qui influencent l’horizon d’investissement et la tolérance au risque. Considérer la sécurité foncière comme une simple variable de contrôle revient à négliger cette interaction fondamentale.

Principales recommandations

En définitive, l’étude montre que la sécurité foncière joue un rôle déterminant dans la relation entre le financement agricole et l’adoption des innovations technologiques. Elle contribue à la littérature sur les systèmes d’innovation agricole en Afrique de l’Ouest en soulignant que l’inclusion financière ne se traduit pas nécessairement par une innovation inclusive lorsque les droits fonciers ne sont pas suffisamment sécurisés.

Ces enseignements sont particulièrement pertinents pour l’élaboration de politiques visant à atteindre l’autosuffisance rizicole et à renforcer les capacités des petits exploitants dans les économies en développement.

Nos résultats nous conduisent à recommander une approche intégrée associant les politiques de crédit à la réforme foncière, plutôt que des interventions isolées. Améliorer uniquement l’accès au crédit, sans sécuriser les droits fonciers, risque de ne pas favoriser l’adoption des variétés améliorées chez les ménages les plus vulnérables.

À l’inverse, les réformes foncières qui renforcent la reconnaissance officielle des droits ou réduisent les conflits fonciers peuvent accroître la valeur de la terre comme garantie et améliorer l’efficacité du crédit pour financer l’adoption de nouvelles technologies agricoles.

Plus largement, l’étude plaide en faveur de politiques intégrées qui s’attaquent simultanément aux défaillances des marchés du crédit, du foncier et des technologies.

stories.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
stories.summary: The post Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A black-and-white aerial photo of a plant with a tall smokestack and many big and small buildings. It sits in a dry environment next to a wide river.
stories.body:
Co-published with Cascade PBS and KUOW

Reporting Highlights

Toxic Legacy: Workers got sick cleaning up radioactive waste at a former federal nuclear weapons site in Washington, and the state passed a law to make it easier to claim benefits.

Litigating Workers’ Claims: The Department of Energy denies responsibility and has filed more than 500 legal appeals seeking to block state benefits being given to workers and their survivors.

Millions Go to Lawyers: DOE has spent nearly $12 million on outside lawyers and expert testimony to fight state compensation claims.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.

As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.

The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.

“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.

In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

“But that’s not what happens.”

“Depleted and Disgusted”

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”

But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.

The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.

The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.

Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.

“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

“When Does This End?”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.

“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”

Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

The DOE appealed. It hired a medical toxicologist, who reviewed Rouse’s medical records and testified that he did not have the disease he claimed, and brought in an industrial hygienist, who downplayed the exposure risks at Hanford. The DOE’s toxicologist testified that Rouse’s drinking was “the most significant, what we might term, ‘toxic exposure’ that’s described in the medical record.”

A group of three physicians and an industrial hygienist have collectively earned over $1.7 million testifying against Hanford workers since the presumption law’s passage, according to DOE invoices the newsrooms obtained by a federal records request. One of the DOE’s go-to expert witness doctors earned more than $200,000 from the DOE last year alone. He did not respond to multiple emails seeking comment.

A single law firm, Wallace, Mann, Capener, Bishop & Debney, handles all of the DOE’s appeals. In addition to the fees paid to expert witnesses, the department paid the firm nearly $10 million between 2018 and 2025. The law firm did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

In cases where the DOE has appealed the state’s approval of a claim since 2018, the agency that handles appeals has sided with workers nearly 9 times out of 10, according to state data.

Pollet, the state representative who sponsored the 2018 presumption bill, acknowledged that the law has fallen short of his expectation.

“This was supposed to have ended a decade ago,” he said about sick Hanford workers still awaiting back wages and medical care. “It’s even worse than it was 10 years ago.”

“I think their actions are not only despicable, but they are criminal,” he said of the DOE.

The state Department of Labor and Industries said it expected “to engage further with the DOE,” which could include putting the department on an improvement plan and monitoring its progress.

Another option state regulators have is to revoke the DOE’s ability to accept and pay out claims directly. According to the state Department of Labor and Industries, the contractors that employ Hanford workers on behalf of the DOE would then decide whether to join the state-managed fund or seek state approval to manage claims themselves. Doing so could limit the DOE’s power to appeal, but contractors would still have that right.

Brown, the state attorney general, said he wants to wait and see how the DOE’s appeals of claims play out in higher courts. He hopes that once the DOE’s losses start stacking up, it will slow the volume of its litigation.

Attorney Charlynn Hull said she thought the DOE’s approach might soften during the Biden administration. But Hull said she observed no change in the DOE’s behavior. Her firm, Smart Law, represents the majority of Hanford workers’ compensation claimants, including Rouse and Kersey.

One of the hardest things about the DOE’s appeals, Hull said, is the testifying that the children and spouses of dead workers must do.

“I think that it’s just, it’s tormenting to them, in many ways, to relive how awful that experience was, especially with the cancer-related death,” Hull said. “When does this end?”

Dying While Under Appeal

For Isidoro Mata Jr., it ended with his children draining fluid from his lungs through a tube doctors had surgically inserted into his chest.

Mata demolished buildings at Hanford for nearly 30 years. Court records show he was diagnosed in 2015 with thyroid cancer, one of the illnesses that Washington’s law ties to work at Hanford. Sara Chilcoat, his daughter, said he kept working as long as he could.

State claims managers approved Mata’s claim in 2019. The DOE appealed, arguing that “medical opinion supports denial of this claim as not related to the distinctive conditions of employment.” The appeal did not elaborate further. The state forced the DOE to pay his wages and the cost of his medications, Chilcoat said. But the DOE filed a separate motion to stop his benefits while the appeal was adjudicated.

In its motion, the DOE argued that it was likely to prevail in its appeal because a doctor who examined Mata in 2019 believed his cancer was unrelated to his work at Hanford, according to court records. The state found the doctor’s examination “lacking in objective findings.”

“He was fighting for his life while they were trying to do that,” Chilcoat said. “That makes me mad.”

Mata’s case file notes that he missed three meetings with DOE lawyers in 2020. The state attorney general’s office sent the appeals judge a letter in July explaining that Mata was unable to participate because of his chemotherapy treatments. The DOE, which did not respond to questions about Mata’s case, dropped its appeal in December.

Less than three months later, Mata died.

stories.title: Arms Control, not Ukraine, Should Be on the Superpower Agenda
stories.summary: The proposed meeting of Trump, Putin, and Xi nex month in Shenzhen could make real progress on arms control—as long as it steers clear of the Ukraine war. The post Arms Control, not Ukraine, Should Be on the Superpower Agenda appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Asked at the White House whether he would sit down with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, Donald Trump steered the conversation from Ukraine to warheads. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he said. Russia, he added, “has been fine on Ukraine.” In the same exchange he suggested it was time for someone other than Volodymyr Zelensky to negotiate for Kyiv.

Two proposals now ride on one invitation. Putin, according to The Wall Street Journal , pitched the meeting as a way to end the war on terms that favor Moscow. Trump pitched it as arms control. Only one of them belongs in Shenzhen.

The summit itself is worth holding. The two largest nuclear arsenals have gone more than eight months without a single binding limit since New START expired on February 5. Trump turned down Putin’s offer to observe its ceilings voluntarily for another year, saying he wanted a better treaty. He has no better treaty. He has a venue.

The objection is easy to predict: China will refuse to play. Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman, Mao Ning , said last week that asking China to join trilateral disarmament talks “at this stage” is “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic,” and that the United States carries “special and primary responsibility.” In Washington, that line will be interpreted as obstruction.

Read the numbers before reading the motive. SIPRI’s latest yearbook puts the U.S. military stockpile at 3,700 warheads and Russia’s at 4,400. China holds about 620 . Even if Beijing passes 1,000 by 2030, SIPRI notes, it would have about a quarter of either arsenal. Russia and the United States control roughly 83 percent of the world’s usable warheads.

A negotiation that asks the smallest of the three to freeze first is not arms control. It asks China to accept permanent inferiority as the entry fee. When Washington and Moscow signed SALT I in 1972, nobody asked Britain, France, or China to sign too.

However, China’s arsenal is growing faster than anyone’s. SIPRI estimates that Beijing may now have around 34 warheads deployed with operational forces, up from 24, and it has loaded missiles into three new silo fields. Washington’s worry is not invented.

Three things could come out of that room that none of the three leaders would have to sell at home as a defeat.

The first would be a restored ceiling. Washington and Moscow can announce that they will observe New START’s central limit of 1,550 deployed strategic warheads for 12 months and resume data exchanges. Russia has already said that it would keep to those limits if the United States does. The pledge costs Trump nothing, and the Arms Control Association has suggested the three leaders could reaffirm their test-ban commitments in the same statement.

Second, China could offer something that corresponds to the size of its arsenal. Beijing has held to a no-first-use pledge since its first test in 1964 and has pressed the other nuclear powers for years to adopt one as well. A three-way reaffirmation of the January 2022 statement by the five nuclear powers that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, paired with a leaders’ hotline and missile-launch notifications among the three, would bring China into a risk-reduction process without asking it to cap an arsenal that’s a fraction of the others. That is a track Beijing can accept, and the host of the summit has every reason to want it to work.

Third, the leaders could agree to a written firewall. The communiqué should state plainly that Ukrainian territory is not on the Shenzhen agenda. Here Beijing’s own record helps. China’s February 2023 position paper on the war opened with respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries. On Monday, Mao Ning said that the ministry had no information about any trilateral meeting. Beijing has shown no appetite for hosting the carve-up of a third country, and it has every interest in a Shenzhen summit remembered for warheads rather than borders.

The firewall matters because the alternative is already visible. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha , warned that a meeting of the three without Kyiv would “encourage Putin to continue this war.” The day after Trump called Russia “fine,” a Russian drone strike near the Kyiv-Odesa highway killed three people . The Washington Post reported that the administration has not approved the interceptors Kyiv needs.

A summit that swaps arms control for Ukrainian land would hand Putin the prize his army has failed to take, and it would discredit the nuclear track for a generation.

From Karachi, the picture is less abstract. The big three are not the only problem. SIPRI counts India at 190 warheads and Pakistan at about 170 , and in May 2025 the two traded missile and drone strikes in the heaviest fire between nuclear-armed neighbors in decades. A Shenzhen deal will freeze nothing below the top tier. It would at least show that great powers can still sign something. South Asia has not seen such an example in a long time.

Trump likes to say he ends wars. He has a better chance of ending an arms race that has run without rules since February, and he can do it in a city whose host wants the meeting to succeed.

The test will be visible when APEC closes on November 19 . If the Shenzhen statement carries the number 1,550, the summit will have done what no arms control meeting has managed in five years. If it carries the word Ukraine without a Ukrainian in the room, it will be remembered as Yalta with a nuclear footnote.

stories.title: The Next Minab
stories.summary: More important than who is right in a war is who is next: the child at the next school desk, the family in the next building, the stranger on the next flight. The post The Next Minab appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A group of women gather by a grave to mourn at the cemetery of Minab City on May 14, 2026 in Minab, Iran.(Majid Saeedi/Getty Images)

On a recent Piers Morgan show , the guest was Robert Pape, a University of Chicago political scientist. The subject was a set of wars that now feed each other: Russia and Ukraine, the Yemen and Saudi Arabia, the United States and Israel against Iran.

Pape, who founded the Chicago Project on Security and Threats, turned to the danger of moral certainty in war. He began with the protesters killed in Iran:

Whether the numbers are several thousand protesters that were killed by the Iran regime, or higher than that, the fact of the matter is, killing protesters is not something we think of as just OK.

Then he asked how wars cross their own thresholds:

How do you break thresholds and get cycles of violence? Where you get wars of the cities, … and how you get this is moral certainty on each side, which causes then civilians to be attacked more and more and more aggressively as if they (the civilians) deserve it.

His research on suicide terrorism, in Dying to Win and Cutting the Fuse , finds foreign occupation to be the leading driver. “Moral certainty is the fuel for the escalation trap,” he said, naming the framework he uses to anticipate how wars widen.

Moral certainty identifies who is to blame. It cannot predict who is about to get hurt.

What Is Documented, What Is Not

On February 28, the first day of the Iran war, a missile hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, in southern Iran. The AP counts about 120 children among the dead, Iranian state media put the total at 168, and AFP reported at least 155 killed, most of them children. Reporters have had limited access, so the exact toll is still disputed.

The school stood beside a Revolutionary Guard compound, visibly separated from it since 2016. The Congressional Research Service reports that a Tomahawk hit the school and that a preliminary U.S. military investigation found the United States responsible, working from outdated targeting information. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States “would not deliberately target a school.” Months later, AP reported that the Pentagon had still not published its findings.

The details that stay with me are small ones. The AP found that teachers phoned parents to collect their children before Iran’s government ordered schools closed that morning, and some parents did not make it in time.

You can blame Tehran’s repression and its nuclear program, or you can blame Washington’s decision to strike. Either way, the children in that building chose neither, were responsible for neither, and paid the ultimate price.

Minab was also not the last time. In early September, Reuters reported that Iran counted 18 civilians dead in U.S. strikes, including four at a wedding, and the UN secretary general said he was deeply alarmed. Iranian missiles and drones have also hit Gulf cities, with airport strikes in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Civilians on every side of this war have paid for decisions they did not make.

The Next Building

On PBS’s Amanpour & Company on March 25, Robert Pape said that “even with smart bombs, there’s going to be collateral damage of a serious nature,” and that the anger it leaves behind has consequences: “we are setting in train exactly the anger for how you get indiscriminate terrorism and you get people willing to die (in order) to kill.” In his weekly Escalation Trap conversations, he has said he expects that the next wave of violence will come from inspired attackers rather than centrally directed ones.

The distinction matters. Counterterrorism scholar Bruce Hoffman told KERA’s Think on March 18 that in the war’s first nine days, “we’ve seen three serious attacks in the United States, one in Austin, of course, where two people were murdered,” and that the attackers seemed “completely self-motivated outside any kind of identifiable terrorist command and control chain.”

The Austin gunman killed two people and wounded 14 on March 1. He wore a shirt with an Iranian flag, and the FBI said it was investigating terror links , but police said it was too early to name a motive, and an internal counterterrorism update noted a history of mental health conditions. In mid-March, a man drove a vehicle into Temple Israel , a synagogue near Detroit, with about 140 people inside, roughly 106 of them children; no attendees were reported hurt. An anonymous Lebanese official told the AP that the attacker’s two brothers and their two children had died in an Israeli strike days earlier. The AP could not verify that, and officials had not established a motive.

Neither case proves that the war caused the violence. There is also a serious counterargument: CSIS analyst Daniel Byman noted in April that Iran has not used terrorism in this war, and offered several explanations, including lost capacity, fear of escalation and the usefulness of missiles and shipping disruption. He also warned that this restraint may be a pause, not an ending. The American Conservative likewise argued that Iran has few incentives to orchestrate attacks, while Hoffman warned that the risk of lone-actor incidents rises the longer the war lasts. The dispute is about who and when. Almost no one claims that the risk shrinks as the war goes on.

Nor does the harm stop at Iran’s borders. In Yemen, the UN human rights chief said on September 24 that civilians are “bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting,” with 32 civilians killed since August, 15 of them children. In Ukraine, the UN has documented 15,280 civilians killed or injured in the first eight months of 2026.

Why Diplomacy Loses the Room

On September 17, the UN’s fact-finding mission on Iran found reasonable grounds to believe that U.S. forces committed war crimes in two February strikes, including Minab. It said the school was clearly civilian, that the intelligence behind the strike was not adequately verified, and that the attack went beyond negligence. In the same report, the mission found that Iran’s crackdown on protesters since late December amounted to crimes against humanity. Iran’s own official toll is 3,038 dead, which the mission believes understates the real number.

Both findings stand together. The U.S. government has not accepted the first: President Trump said in June that “nobody” purposely attacked the school, and the Pentagon has not published its findings. Anyone who wants a single villain has to look away from one of them. That is exactly what Pape meant by moral certainty. Each side sees only the victims the other side made.

Speed is the second problem. The Pentagon relied on an AI targeting platform called Maven to strike more than 13,000 targets in the first 38 days of the war. “For U.S. military officials, Maven’s speed in selecting and reselecting targets represents a distinct combat advantage, allowing U.S. forces to disable Iranian combat capabilities swiftly and incessantly, preventing their reconstitution,” writes Michael Klare at Arms Control Today . Politico reported in March that Pentagon staff focused on reducing civilian casualties had fallen from about 200 to fewer than 40. One former official told the AP that the Minab strike was a natural result of those cuts and of Secretary Hegseth’s emphasis on lethality.

Early in the war, Hegseth said that the operation was “just getting started” and “accelerating not decelerating.” Force comes with a slogan and a victory lap. Diplomacy comes with compromise, and compromise has no one to cheer it. A debate about who is right will always make more noise than a question about who is next.

What It Would Take

Five shifts would help in preventing the next Minab.

It’s important to change the first question. Hosts and producers of news programs can ask “who is most likely to be hurt next, and what would stop it?” before they ask “who is right?” They can seat civilian-protection investigators, humanitarian workers, and mediators beside the partisans. They should likewise make civilian harm a standing story. Minab returns to the headlines only when a new document leaks. Washington cannot keep ignoring Minab, but to do so lawmakers and citizens must demand accountability. An independent review and a public explanation must be required after there is credible evidence of grave harm from an AI-assisted targeting system.

To fight against amnesia, it’s critical to remember the names of the victims. The AP calls the ruined school in Minab a memorial: “This will never be a school again.” In March, Win Without War laid children’s backpacks on Capitol Hill for the dead. Ordinary people can keep such memorials in front of lawmakers who would rather not look.

Diplomacy is essential. A Pakistan-brokered ceasefire in April, which FPIF’s Imran Khalid described as “a shift in the center of the diplomatic world,” showed that diplomacy can still find a way. Pape has said that a deal resembling the 2015 nuclear agreement is still possible, with low enrichment, sanctions relief and inspections. Voters can tell their representatives that this is the outcome they want.

Finally, multiple truths must be upheld simultaneously. The UN found grounds for war crimes at Minab and crimes against humanity against Iranian protesters. Saying so is accuracy, not equivalence, and it is the primary method of challenging the moral certainty that Pape describes.

The next building is somewhere. It is not yet a headline. There’s still time to make sure it never becomes one.

stories.title: Long After Maui Fire, Residents Found With High Levels of Toxic Metals in Their Bodies
stories.summary: More than a year after a devastating wildfire destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina, residents were found to have high levels of arsenic and other toxic metals in their bodies. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by Grist , in partnership with The Intercept , and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Damage from the 2023 fire that destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina. Matt McClain / The Washington Post via Getty Images via Grist

More than a year after a devastating wildfire destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina, residents were found to have high levels of arsenic and other toxic metals in their bodies.

In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions of dollars in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Indigenous Kanaka Maoli and cofounder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lahaina, including doctors, nurses, and therapists.

Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said.

The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that more than 1 in 5 residents had reduced lung function.

Now, new research from the same project has found elevated levels of toxic metals in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.

“What we consider and sometimes look at as a one-time event isn’t really one-time anymore,” Alika Maunakea, who is Kanaka Maoli and codirector of MauiWES, told Grist .

Researchers don’t yet know how much of the contamination came from the fires and how much was already present in the environment. That distinction matters as wildfires increasingly race through towns like Lahaina and cities like Los Angeles, where burning of homes, cars, and infrastructure can leave contaminants that people encounter for months or years afterward.

“We have traditionally thought about wildfire exposure primarily through the lens of smoke,” Maunakea said in a press release. “But when an entire community burns, we are dealing with a much more complicated exposure environment.” Researchers must also understand what contaminants were already present, what the fire may have released, and what entered residents’ bodies, he said.

The research, which studied 1,400 adults across Maui six to 18 months after the fires, measured 24 metals in urine samples. It found that participants had higher concentrations of several metals than people in a nationwide health survey conducted before the fires. That included 2.2 times as much arsenic, 2.3 times as much barium, and 3.8 times as much manganese. Antimony, which is used in flame retardant materials and has been previously linked to lung irritation, stomach pain, and other symptoms, was found at levels nearly 40 times higher.

Because the researchers lack comparable data from before the fires, they could not determine how much of the metal exposure resulted from the disaster. Maunakea told Grist that answering that question is the next step for the project, which has received a $3.6 million grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. That work will include investigating whether and to what degree past agricultural and industrial activity contributed to the contamination.

“It’s important to realize that these are all part of settler colonialism,” Ahia said. “So what we’re looking at is confounding factors that are to the detriment of the health of our local people.”

Decades of plantation agriculture altered water systems, introduced herbicides, and displaced native plants, leaving a legacy on the islands that is still felt today. Disasters like fires and storms can compound those ongoing environmental problems.

“If we begin the story when the fire starts, we miss the decisions that shaped the landscape and the community’s ability to respond,” said Katie Kamelamela, who is Indigenous Kanaka Maoli and an assistant professor at Arizona State University based in Hawaii. “Micro climate change acts on places already shaped by histories of land ownership, water diversion, development, and unequal access to resources.”

Kamelamela said true recovery must look beyond the fire. “I want recovery to be measured by whether people can remain in their communities, care for ʻāina, and pass on their knowledge and practices in place,” she said, using the Hawaiian word for land, which carries deeper meaning and relationship than property or mere place. “Rebuilding should not recreate the same conditions that left people at risk. Caring for ʻāina and caring for people need to be funded and planned together.”

Maunakea said the multitude of intersecting pressures is one reason why he wanted to pursue this research. As climate change continues to accelerate, longstanding issues facing Native Hawaiians like housing, the harms of tourism, and the legacy of plantations can amplify problems. “We worry that disasters like this that we experience on Maui, as well as the floods and other storms that we’re experiencing now, is just going to continue widening the gaps in health disparities that already exist in those populations,” he said.

Moving forward, the project will not just identify health risks but also help residents respond to them. Study participants receive their results, discuss them, and meet with health professionals. “People now know that there’s these types of potential hazards, and what to do about them is a big concern,” Maunakea said. “We still don’t have all the answers for sure, but we are taking the next steps to get a better picture and inform our community around it.”

— Joseph Lee , Grist

stories.body:

ANALYSIS

After decades of losses, mangrove trees are gaining ground on coastlines around the world, often in places they have never grown before. Paradoxically, scientists say, warming temperatures and the destruction of inland forests are helping to power the revival.

By Fred Pearce • October 22, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

From the bayous of Louisiana to the backwaters of the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, from the lagoons of West Africa to the billabongs of northern Australia, mangroves are making a dramatic and unexpected comeback.

What a difference a couple of decades can make.

In 2007, ecologists from six countries asked in a letter published in the journal Science whether we would soon be living in “a world without mangroves.” One of the world’s most distinctive, biodiverse, and carbon-rich ecosystems was in rapid retreat in the face of encroaching agriculture, construction of sea walls, ports, and marinas, and rising sea levels. The mangroves seemed doomed.

But in recent months two separate studies have painted a very different picture. A high-resolution analysis of satellite imagery published in Science in June found that the stunted, salt-tolerant trees are now undergoing an “unexpected expansion,” healing after decades of destruction.

At the same time, a report on the State of the World’s Mangroves , published in September by a group of NGOs under the umbrella of the Global Mangrove Alliance, found that “mangroves are now increasing in extent, year on year,” said coauthor Mark Spalding of The Nature Conservancy.

For the first time, mangrove forests are expanding faster than they are declining, says a coastal ecologist.

It’s not that the destruction of mangroves has ended. But the Science study finds that new mangrove growth between 2010 and 2023 covered approximately 3,200 square miles, outpacing losses of around 2,400 square miles. Worldwide, mangrove cover is now back to the levels last seen in the 1980s.

The new findings are the surprising outcome of the most detailed analysis yet attempted of satellite imagery of mangroves over the past four decades, says Pete Bunting, a remote sensing analyst at Aberystwyth University in Wales, who worked on both studies. It shows that previous assessments had provided “a substantial underestimation of mangrove gains” over the past 15 years, says the Science study’s lead author Zhen Zhang of Tulane University in Louisiana.

“For the first time, these unique ecosystems are expanding at a faster rate than they are declining,” says Catherine Lovelock, a coastal ecologist at the University of Queensland, who was not involved in either study.

However, not all ecologists are celebrating.

For one thing, mangroves are recovering in some places thanks to environmental degradation elsewhere. For another, says Norman Duke, an ecologist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and lead author of the 2007 letter, mangrove quantity should not be confused with quality. Lost old-growth mangrove forests, which harbor the most wildlife, are being replaced by less biodiverse and resilient new stands, he says. Contrary to the new studies, “the world’s mangroves are not bouncing back.”

A coral reef around the roots of mangrove trees in Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Wendy Mitchell / Mangrove Photography Awards 2026

Mangroves are unique trees, evolved with specialized roots that anchor in shallow, intertidal waters with slow currents, no frost, and plenty of sediment. Mangrove forests are critical biodiversity hotspots, supporting everything from barnacles to tigers, and are vital fish nurseries for the oceans. For coastal communities, they yield rich harvests of crabs and shellfish and form a protective barrier, absorbing winds and tidal surges during storms, and even moderating the energy of tsunamis. They also store large amounts of carbon — typically four times more than nearby tropical rainforests.

Zhang has recorded the biggest revivals in the river estuaries of northern Australia and river deltas in India. In each case, the new growth extends across more than 450 square miles. But the most surprising turnaround has been in Southeast Asian countries, which were once the scene of rapid mangrove destruction. Since 2010, they have accounted for more than 40 percent of global gains.

Myanmar is “still the most severely deforested country among major mangrove-holding nations,” says Zhang. But since 2010, its mangroves have grown in area by 10 percent. Indonesia tells a similar story. After major losses in past decades, due primarily to a boom in shrimp and fish aquaculture, mangroves have been stable since 2005, when the boom began to abate. The country remains home to around a quarter of the world’s mangroves.

“Some 65 percent of mangrove gains are in new places where mangroves have not grown before,” says an analyst.

So, what is going on? Why the dramatic upturn for a global ecosystem once considered all but doomed by human invasion and rising seas? The new remote-sensing analysis, despite its greater resolution, allows only tentative conclusions. “We don’t fully understand what is driving these gains,” says Bunting. His mapping cannot distinguish planted trees from natural recovery, for instance. But there is growing evidence that natural regeneration is powering the resurgence.

Sometimes, mangroves are recolonizing areas previously taken by humans but since abandoned. During the late 20th century, coastal communities across the tropics ripped out millions of acres of mangroves in East and Southeast Asia alone to make way for ponds where they raised fish and shrimp for lucrative international markets. But many of these ponds soon became unproductive through disease, pollution, or poor management, and were abandoned.

But such recolonization is only part of the story. “Some 65 percent of mangrove gains are in new places where mangroves have not grown before,” the State of the World’s Mangroves report finds. Sometimes climate change is helping extend the range of mangroves polewards. On the Mississippi Delta, they are overtaking salt marshes as warmer winters eliminate mangrove-killing frosts, restricting habitat for birds and foraging mammals that need open ground.

False-color satellite images show the growth of mangroves at the mouth of the Matamuhuri River in Bangladesh between 1990 and 2023. Source: Landsat imagery. Courtesy of Pete Bunting

The majority of the gains, however, “seem to occur in river mouths and deltas and are being driven by sediment coming off the land,” says Bunting. On reaching the ocean, the sediment settles, creating mudbanks that mangroves swiftly colonize. The unsettling paradox is that, in many cases, mangroves along coastlines are returning thanks to the destruction of their forest counterparts inland. The loss of trees and their roots destabilizes soils, causing erosion and the flow of sediment into rivers.

That is what has happened along the Yangon estuary in southern Myanmar. Part of the giant Irrawaddy Delta, the estuary stretches some 25 miles from the ocean to the country’s biggest city, Yangon. The estuary lost more than half its mangroves between 1988 and 2011 as rice farmers moved onto its shores and replaced mangroves with rice fields, erecting dikes to protect them from the salty water. But the mangroves have since made a dramatic comeback. By 2023, their coverage had increased almost tenfold to more than 13,000 acres, according to Phyu Phway Thant of the Myanmar Maritime University in Thanlyin, who has mapped the growth from satellite imagery.

The rice fields have not gone. Instead, almost all the growth was mangroves colonizing new mudbanks created from sediment dislodged by upstream sand mining and deforestation, which was driven by illegal logging and the expansion of agriculture along tributaries of the Yangon River.

Millions of dollars have been spent planting mangroves, but most of these projects have failed, a report found.

This is not unusual. The growth of mudbanks in many estuaries has coincided with an increase in sediment brought down by rivers to coastal waters over the last 20 years, says the State of the World’s Mangroves report. Other examples include parts of the giant Amazon Delta in Brazil, the shores of peninsular Malaysia, and the North Island of New Zealand, which is at the southernmost limit of potential mangrove habitat.

“Rising sea levels should in theory restrict mangrove growth, as seas invade the intertidal areas where they grow,” says Lovelock, but at the mouths of many rivers, sediment deposition is creating land faster than the seas are engulfing it, creating new habitats that mangroves swiftly colonize. And once established, the dense networks of mangrove roots trap more sediment — enough, the State of the World’s Mangroves report concludes, to keep pace with current rising tides in many places.

Of course, this positive feedback loop can be confounded by upstream dams, which drastically reduce the amount of sediment being carried toward the ocean, stopping the growth of intertidal mud flats, and causing deltas to be drowned.

Shrimp farms in Prachuap Khiri Khan province in Thailand have displaced mangrove forests. Ingram Publishing

For this reason, there are serious concerns among ecologists about the fate of East Africa’s largest expanse of mangroves, on the delta of the River Rufiji in Tanzania. In recent years, new mangrove stands have grown on mudflats in the outer delta, says Bunting. But that growth could now abruptly halt. In August, the Tanzanian government completed the Julius Nyerere hydroelectric dam some 100 miles upstream. The environmental group WWF has estimated that the dam will trap most of the 16.6 million tons of sediment flowing down the river each year — initiating a cycle of delta retreat and mangrove loss.

The growth of new mangrove stands has been accompanied by a growing awareness among some governments and coastal communities of their value. This is especially true in Indonesia and other countries bordering the Indian Ocean that were hit by a tsunami in 2004 that killed more than 200,000 people. Villages that had kept their mangroves were much better protected than those that had converted them to fishponds.

A resulting fashion for planting new mangroves has had mixed results, however. Tens of millions of dollars have been spent on planting mangroves across the tropics in recent years, according to the NGO Wetlands International. But “the majority of these restoration projects have failed,” it said in a recent report. More than 80 percent of seedlings have died or been washed away by the tides.

The new mangrove stands colonizing the tropics may not be as resilient as their predecessors, an ecologist warns.

In response, some conservation groups have begun helping communities manage coastal landscapes to encourage natural regeneration. On the north shore of Java, villagers have erected some 10 miles of near-shore brushwood barriers to create calm water where seedlings cast off by mangroves have become established.

And in the West African state of Guinea-Bissau, Wetlands International is recruiting locals to encourage the natural return of mangroves to abandoned rice fields. “We open up dikes and clean the old natural canals” to allow water carrying mangrove seedlings from nearby stands to return, says Abdoulaye Ndiaye, who runs the program. Nature does the rest. More than 6,000 acres have been restored since 2015.

Meanwhile, the greener landscapes seen in satellite images do not necessarily indicate that biodiversity has recovered, says Uday Pimple of King Mongkut’s University of Technology in Bangkok, who has been doing extensive field research in the mangrove swamps of Thailand.

In Phang Nga province in western Thailand — an area where tin mining, charcoal burning, and shrimp farming previously decimated coastal mangroves — he found that 90 percent of mangrove recovery since the 1980s has been through the natural regeneration of a range of mangrove species, creating biodiverse forest. But restored mangrove forests in Trat province in eastern Thailand, which appear identical on satellite images, were largely planted with a single species of mangrove, resulting in much less biodiversity.

A man plants mangrove seedlings in Banda Aceh, Indonesia. Hand-planted mangroves rarely reach maturity. Chaideer Mahyuddin / AFP via Getty Images

Clearly, the prognosis for mangroves remains contested. Bunting says, “It is quite possible that the future trend will be similar to the last 15 years,” with gains continuing to exceed losses. And in a study of the likely fate of mangroves in a world 2 degrees Celsius warmer, Daniel Friess, a colleague of Zhang at Tulane University, found reasons to believe the trees could thrive. Because, at least in some places, they seem well able to keep pace with rising sea levels. Because increased rainfall will often increase soil erosion inland and sediment deposition along shorelines, giving mangroves even more room to expand. And because warmer temperatures should push mangroves further outside the tropics, replacing many more salt marshes in Australia and the southern U.S., for instance, for better or for worse.

But Duke argues that the new mangrove stands colonizing the tropics may not be as resilient as their predecessors to the more severe weather triggered by climate change. Or as useful in capturing and holding onto carbon. “They are immature stands, not fully developed in either biomass or biodiversity,” he says. That will leave them ever more vulnerable “as damaging [weather] events become more severe and more frequent.” Recent research appears to support his pessimistic presumption.

Field studies in China’s Hainan province found that mature mangrove forests recovered much more quickly from tropical cyclones, with their high winds, strong rainfall, and storm surges, compared with younger forests. The researchers stressed the importance of protecting old-growth mangroves rather than relying on new stands to replace them. Without such a strategy, humanity may yet face what Duke feared: “a world without mangroves.”
