Lib Dem Richmond council leader Gareth Roberts said the cuts risked "pushing this council towards a financial cliff edge".

He said: "We will not stand by while Whitehall forces our residents to pay the price for a deeply flawed formula."

Tory Kensington and Chelsea council leader Elizabeth Campbell said: "I will use every tool at my disposal to fight these cuts, stand up for our residents and secure the fair deal our borough deserves."

A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson previously said: "We have consulted extensively on reforming the outdated council funding system to ensure money goes where it is most needed, following on from a longstanding consensus.

"We're also protecting councils through transitional arrangements so no area faces a cliff edge."

stories.title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
stories.summary: The Tory leader calls for more support for police officers and the public when they step in to help.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch speaking at the Police Federation conference in London

Published 22 October 2026

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.

Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.

Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.

The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.

In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.

"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.

"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."

The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper , killed investigating a quad bike theft.

She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba , who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.

The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".

Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.

"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."

Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.

"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."

The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

stories.body:
Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears grow

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns.

The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day.

And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June.

Jim Reid , of Deutsche Bank , says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market:

double quotation mark As storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020. Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl. So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024.

And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says:

double quotation mark …In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%. Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya , an analyst at Swissquote , says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting.

double quotation mark Given the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst. These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found.

Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft , Google , Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results.

Elsewhere this morning , British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%.

An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said :

double quotation mark The drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end. At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October. But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role.

The agenda

7am BST: British retail sales

9am BST: Flash PMI for Eurozone

9.30am BST: Flash PMI for UK, construction statistics for Great Britain 2025

11.30am BST: Russia’s interest rate decision

3pm BST: Flash PMI for US, University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence index

US stocks are poised to fall when the market opens later this afternoon, with futures for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq down.

Susannah Streeter , of the broker Wealth Club, adds that the prospect of higher borrowing costs will unsettle investors betting on companies that are spending huge amounts on AI.

double quotation mark Investors have turned highly nervous again about the cost of the build out, and there’s likely to be little comeback today for tech stocks which have been severely tested this week. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.6% to 26,009 and the S&P 500 fell 1.2% [on Thursday]. Futures markets point to a muted start for Wall Street with few sparks of hope around to ignite a meaningful recovery.

Boom in weight-loss drugs could trigger drop in beer sales, Heineken says

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.

The world’s second largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month warning that GLP-1 use – led by Ozempic and Wegovy – can reduce the desire to drink alcohol , which could lead to “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars.

The document, revealed by Reuters , warned that the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.

GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick, easy solution to rapid weight loss , with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan .

Heineken, the world’s second largest brewer after AB InBev , said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits are evolving.

Rob Wood , chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, says the biggest news is from S&P’s PMI data is the composite employment index rising above 50 for the first time since the 2024 budget.

He said:

double quotation mark The jobs balance rose to 50.5 from 48.9 in September, consistent with a 9K month-to-month payrolls gain in October. Solid growth is helping, probably alongside an easing drag from the payroll-tax hike. …The steady recovery in jobs growth further undermines any case for waiting to hike rates. A November rate hike is a shoo-in, and we expect another rone in February. We are very close to adding a third hike in May or earlier. It’s a really close call, but at the margin, we hold off after weak consumer signals this morning. It would take little—small further energy price rises, a hawkish DMP—to push us to three hikes.

UK business activity growth accelerates to fastest since February

Some good news amid the doom and gloom this morning – UK business activity growth has accelerated to its fastest since February, helped by rebound in new orders, according to a survey published this morning.

The preliminary S&P Global UK composite purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 53.1 in October, higher than forecast and up from 52.0 in September.

A number of businesses cited a boost to sales from AI investment spending and rising demand for technology services, according to the survey. However, it found there will still many reports of sales being affected by geopolitical uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Weaker demand was evident in the construction and real estate sectors in particular, it found.

But Chris Williamson , chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , said that the survey also showed that businesses were taking on additional workers for the first time since hiring fell after the autumn budget of 2024.

double quotation mark There are reports of paused spending due to a lack of clarity on domestic economic policy in the run up to the budget, meaning the promising economic picture from the latest PMIs should provide an encouraging base for further robust economic growth through the winter months, barring any adverse surprises to businesses in the tax and spending review. Geopolitics, and notably the potential for conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine to add to energy market volatility, are, however, clearly still unsettling many businesses, and cost of living concerns and broader fiscal worries are being compounded by the shift to higher borrowing costs. Price pressures remain worryingly elevated, not only making a rate hike from the Bank of England at its upcoming policy meeting a near certainty but also likely shortening the odds of further rate hikes into 2027.”

It is red across the board in the European stock market this morning, though the falls are not steep. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 index is down 0.4%, while the French Cac 40 is down 0.7%. The German Dax is down by 0.6%.

The Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies across the continent, has fallen by 0.4%.

While less red tape will be welcome news for small businesses, the chancellor is still facing pressure from bigger companies in the UK for more support.

Earlier this month some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco , Costa Coffee and the Co-op, met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.

Businesses have asked for a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves , who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay national insurance contributions (Nics) from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment .

They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.

Government says it will 'slash red tape' to save businesses £800m

The UK government has promised it will “slash red tape” for businesses, in reforms it claims will save firms across the country £800m in administrative and tariff costs per year.

The changes will make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses, it said.

It comes as pressure grows on prime minister Andy Burnham and chancellor John Healey to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK ahead of the budget next week.

The government has set itself a target of reducing the administrative burden of regulation on businesses by 25% by the end of the current parliament.

Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds are scheduled to meet with small business leaders at No 10 North today, where they are expected to accept recommendations from the Small Business Taskforce.

Burnham said in a statement:

double quotation mark It’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street. So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow. Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.”

Healey said :

double quotation mark British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses. That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

Rain Newton-Smith , chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said that the changes were a “welcome step towards giving smaller firms more time and headroom to focus on their businesses.”

double quotation mark The test now is delivery. Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.”

Brent crude hits $114 a barrel

And pressure continues to build this morning, with oil prices rising again . Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is up 1% this morning to $114 a barrel – its highest level since May.

Richard Hunter , of the broker Interactive Investor , points out that oil is now up by about 60% since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and up around 90% in the year so far.

double quotation mark Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.

Susannah Streeter , of the broker Wealth Club , says fears are rising that American and Israeli forces will be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US mid-term elections.

double quotation mark At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still be fired. Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries is adding to supply concerns. The deteriorating situation is once again fanning inflation fears, with companies unlikely to keep absorbing higher energy and freight costs. The longer the conflicts rage, the greater the chance of higher prices becoming more embedded in the economy, and that’s why bets have increased on central banks hiking rates more rapidly.

UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

Neil Bellamy , consumer insights director at GfK , said:

double quotation mark Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

Gloomy picture for retailers in Christmas quarter, economists warn

Economists are warning there could be more gloom ahead for retailers as they enter into the crucial final quarter of the year – which includes Christmas.

Paul Dales , chief UK economist at Capital Economics , said:

double quotation mark October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner. In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole. That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%. This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK , noted that fashion retailers had fared the worst in September, despite the warm weather.

double quotation mark Although all other retail categories saw sales rise year-on-year, rising petrol prices meant that consumers had to divert more of their spending on filling up their cars – over 30% more than last September - meaning less to spend on other things. So, while retail prices, and grocery prices in particular, have remained subdued thanks to industry competition and the delayed pass-through of cost increases due to the conflict in the Middle East, the higher-than-expected inflation reported earlier this week will inevitably translate into less in shoppers’ pockets in the critical run-up to Christmas. With most retailers’ sales coming in the last three months of the year, the upcoming peak season remains on a knife edge. This time last year, uncertainty surrounding the late budget at the end of November held back spending in the preceding two months. While that makes this year’s comparisons easier, retailers will be hoping that anything announced by the Chancellor this year does not add further to their cost of doing business nor dent consumers’ sentiment, which already seems to have fallen from the highs at the end of summer.”

Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears grow

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns.

The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day.

And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June.

Jim Reid , of Deutsche Bank , says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market:

double quotation mark As storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020. Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl. So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024.

And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says:

double quotation mark …In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%. Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya , an analyst at Swissquote , says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting.

double quotation mark Given the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst. These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found.

Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft , Google , Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results.

Elsewhere this morning , British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%.

An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said :

double quotation mark The drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end. At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October. But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role.

stories.body:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans

J ack Price joined the Marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on themeter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.

Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”

For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.

According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.

For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”

Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.

The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”

On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”

In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.

At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.

Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ‘em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”

Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘ What is going on?’” Price says. “The fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”

T wenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.

Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven, you’ve gotta shut off all these things, and a lot of times it doesn’t completely shut off.”

A few rows down from the Buick were Mike and Kate Landaverde in his-and-hers Honda Civics from the 90s: a barebones CRX coupe called Dirty Gertrude and a slightly less spartan wagon called Tatiana. The couple bought them cheap, in keeping with the Y2K ethos. Mike, 34, treats having to bump-start the CRX and his sweat-soaked commutes in summer traffic as part of the thrill ride. “I’m smiling the whole time,” says Mike, who manages a local Wendy’s. They keep a 2021 Toyota Corolla hatchback in the garage as a backstop. That car’s got AC.

When young Wendy’s customers pull up to the drive-through in newer barges he assumes carry huge monthly payments, Mike can’t help feeling a bit smug. The couple’s Hondas, however, haven’t necessarily come cheap. Kate, 39, reckons the money she has put into modifications on Tatiana alone could buy a new car. But the occasional outlays – on an engine swap, most recently – can be done at a self-directed pace. “You can do the mods at your own wallet bracket,” says Kate, a software specialist who does her own wrenching. “You can go eBay parts. But all my friends call me bougie because I’m not gonna do anything cheap.”

Meanwhile, making a case for best in show was Alex Jimenez in a 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan tricked out to look like the Scooby-Doo Mystery Machine. “My family is growing,” said Jimenez, a 32-year-old facilities manager, as his 14-year-old daughter Izel sat shotgun scrolling through her phone while a Scooby-Doo cartoon played on the aftermarket infotainment display. Beyond the extra space, he says, “we love it because I can literally fix everything at home. I don’t need special equipment or tools or a computer to diagnose what’s wrong with it. And it puts smiles on people’s faces everywhere we drive. I mean, everybody’s taking pictures.”

Y2K cars have their charms, sure. Barry, of Consumer Reports calls it “survivorship bias” – seeing the most durable makes and models still on the road contributes to assumptions that all from the era must be rock solid. But there’s a reason the automotive industry moved on. “If you go back to cars in the 1990s, our road-test data and reliability surveys were showing problems that were unheard of on modern vehicles: defective paint, parts falling off; the steering wheel would be on crooked,” Barry says. Rust is another scourge of Y2K cars, though it’s less of a concern in the Sun belt. Newer models are far better protected against corrosion. “The technology that allows a car’s body and frame to survive longer is just so much more advanced,” says Barry, adding that a modern car from a manufacturer that prioritizes reliability can reasonably be expected to last 200,000 miles or more with proper maintenance. To his point: the average car on American roads is now 13 years old .

Still, some young Y2K-car owners welcome the opportunity to get their hands dirty. Che Bidal, a 19-year-old Pit operator who also belongs to the furry community, was idling inside his 2004 Mazda6 as the rain poured on Caffeine and Octane. He takes immense pride in having bought the broken sedan for $900 and getting it running again with another $1,500 in parts and help from AI chatbots and YouTube tutorials. Having Frankensteined a Y2K car back to life, the prospect of taking on a new car payment – in this economy – only to be discouraged by the manufacturer from making his own repairs seems ridiculous. “Car companies are banks now,” says Bidal, who was further emboldened by his positive experience under the hood to start a wrenching group for furries. “Coming from fandom into the [auto enthusiast] community is a whole different thing – pretty amazing.”

Nevertheless, there’s a critical difference between a car that’s gratifying to restore and one that can protect you when something goes terribly wrong. Modern cars are subject to increasingly demanding safety standards, and the differences in structural reinforcements and accident-avoidance features between models just three years apart can be dramatic. Consumer Reports has long recommended that drivers prioritize safety as much as their budget allows – advice that its largely Boomer readership can more easily take aboard, naturally.

Barry went through an old-car phase too. “When I was driving around in my 1988 Renault Medallion, I’d see someone come across the center line as they’re looking on their phone and think, ‘I would not stand a chance in an overlap collision,’” he says. “You might think that the older car you’re driving is a tank. Well, the car might be fine. It’s the things inside the car, the new safety features, that help you survive.” Features like blind-spot monitoring, driver attention monitoring and electric stability control, which intervenes to maintain traction in a skid.

The US auto industry has made some effort to address young consumers’ affordability concerns. In 2021, Ford introduced the Maverick, a four-door compact pickup with an available hybrid powertrain and a starting price below $30,000. A startup called Slate, which offers an infinitely customizable electric truck with a starting price of about $25,000, hopes to begin fulfilling orders at the end of this year.

In China, buyers can get new cars with features that would seem extravagant at the same price point in the US – the payoff from decades of Chinese investment in innovation and American offshoring of manufacturing. An affordable, widely available Chinese car with modern features would give young US car buyers something truly tantalizing to consider. But Chinese automakers are in effect shut out of the US market. Even if they weren’t, Barry cautions: “We’re still not getting one for $8,000. Think closer to $20,000. You’re still going to have a car payment. And even if the interior is simple, it’s a different kind of simplicity than someone driving a 99 Camry is looking for.”

Ultimately, young consumers just want cars that deliver on the industry’s fabled promise of independence – and right now, Y2K cars are meeting the brief. These days, Price’s Pewter Pebble struggles with a leaky sunroof, and the headliner is still drooping. “It’s a Volkswagen so it’s coming back to bite me in the butt,” he says. “I’ve probably had to put three grand into it this year.” But with more than 150,000 miles on the clock, it’s taken him further than even he could have imagined.

The absence of a car note helped him become a homeowner in his 20s. It softened the blow of Alex Vindman’s upset loss to Democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida’s August Senate primary. Rather than scramble for another job, Price took a European vacation to decompress and plot his next move. As it happens, he spoke to the Guardian from the Spanish Pyrenees. “If I had a car payment and I lost my job,” he says, “I wouldn’t have the flexibility to hike a mountain.”

stories.summary: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of defrauding the county council out of thousands of pounds.

stories.body:
Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion

Published 22 October 2026

Ten Ashfield Independent councillors have quit the party this week following the former leader's fraud conviction.

Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion last month

He resigned as leader of Ashfield District Council the following day, but was later given a seat on the authority's planning committee .

As of Thursday, 13 councillors are sitting as non-aligned independents, while 18 Ashfield Independents remain, meaning the party is one councillor away from losing its majority.

Zadrozny was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds.

Prosecutors also alleged that he had failed to pay tax on four rental properties.

The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was told by the judge he would be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence".

The Ashfield Independents now have a majority of one

Councillors Warren Nuttall and Kier Barsby had quit the Ashfield Independents group prior to this week.

One of the 10 members to quit this week is John Wilmott, a cabinet member who is also a Nottinghamshire county councillor for Hucknall North.

Another is the chairman of the council, Dale Grounds.

Councillor Matt Relf, executive lead member for growth, regeneration and local planning, said quitting the party was an "enormously upsetting" decision.

"The understandable controversy around Jason's conviction and the choices he made that led to that have upset and surprised a lot of people in the group," he said.

"With the election of a new leader we hoped that would put everything behind us, but unfortunately the decision to appoint Jason back on to the planning committee was just a step too far.

"That decision was made with no consultation with the broader group.

"To stay true to our principles of integrity and democratic accountability I was left with no option but to leave, and I think others have reached the same conclusion."

Hucknall Central councillor Lee Waters, who was another one of the councillors to quit this week, said his decision "follows a period of reflection, and I believe the time is right to move on".

"Throughout my time as a councillor, my priority has been to listen to residents, address their concerns and work hard on the issues that matter to our community. That remains unchanged," he added.

"I will continue carrying out my council responsibilities and dealing with ongoing casework with the same commitment and dedication as always."

Lee Anderson, the MP for Ashfield, posted on Facebook to warn that former Ashfield Independent councillors would not be accepted into Reform UK.

He said there would be "no deals" between the parties.

Samantha Deakin has taken over as leader of the council, but has so far declined the BBC's request for an interview.

Fiona Fillingham attended the demonstration on Thursday

A demonstration was held outside the council house on Thursday in protest at Zadrozny being able to remain as a council.

Protesters told the BBC they had been "let down" by the authority.

John Green, of the Ashfield Community Action Group, said: "We are disgusted that the Ashfield Independents have voted a convicted fraudster onto the planning a committee."

Tim Curtis, who also attended the demonstration, said: "There's no mechanism to get him out. He should stand down from the council and not be anywhere near making any decisions."

Fiona Fillingham, a local business owner, added: "If I got done for fraud I am sure I wouldn't get my job back.

"It seems backhanded, shoddy, unfair and unrealistic. They can't keep getting away with it."

stories.title: Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
stories.summary: The defence secretary says the UK is "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Rheinmetall said the facility had created 100 jobs and it would look to expand its workforce in the future

Published 22 October 2026

The production of gun barrels to be used on tanks has returned to the UK for the first time in 20 years with the opening of a new manufacturing facility.

The UK Gun Hall in Telford, run by German defence firm Rheinmetall, has supported 100 jobs and will make barrels and breeches for large calibre weapons.

Defence secretary, Wes Streeting, attended the opening ceremony on Thursday and said Britain was "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.

"From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action," he said.

"One hundred skilled jobs in world class manufacturing and the return of large calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in 20 years - this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like," Streeting added.

The barrels and breeches will be made for both 120m and 155mm weapon systems, including for the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms, according to Rheinmetall.

The firm is already involved in the UK's Boxer combat vehicle programme and is upgrading the country's Challenger tanks .

Wes Streeting said the opening of the facility would be a boost to Britain's defence capabilities

Specialist workers from Telford have been recruited and the firm said it would expand its workforce as production ramped up.

Ahead of the factory's opening, staff spent time at a Rheinmetall facility in Germany where they were trained in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production.

Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, said the gun hall was an "important milestone" that would strengthen the country's industrial base "for decades to come".

"We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future," he added.

'Statement of intent'

Papperger told BBC Radio Shropshire it was a significant investment in Telford, adding that the firm only had one similar production line in Germany.

"At the moment, we have a lot of orders and we need the capacity. Telford has very well-educated people, highly-motivated people," he added.

Papperger said the company currently had 1,300 employees in the UK but was looking to build up that number.

During his speech at the event, Streeting described Telford as being "synonymous with engineering and manufacturing".

"Today is a vote of confidence in our country," he continued, "a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country."

stories.title: Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
stories.summary: The softly-spoken former defence secretary is gearing up for the biggest moment of his long political career.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 July 2026

Andy Burnham's decision to appoint John Healey to the crucial role of chancellor of the exchequer was the rarest of things at Westminster - a genuine surprise.

It's not that the 66-year-old lacked experience or credibility - just that he had not been seen as a likely contender, with all the speculation about who would replace Rachel Reeves centring on more high-profile figures.

Healey had flown under the radar since his explosive resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June this year.

His assessment of the government's defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street.

But his resignation letter also included pointed criticism of Reeves's Treasury, which he said had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats".

Now he is in the Treasury hot seat and under pressure to spell out how he will get defence spending up to 3% of national income, at the same time as cutting government borrowing costs and tackling the cost of living.

Like his predecessor, he faces the difficult balancing act of keeping Labour MPs happy without spooking the financial markets, while delivering on the government's key priorities.

Never the flashiest of politicians, his early speeches as chancellor have been focused on stressing his commitment to fiscal discipline and cutting the welfare bill, as well as banging the drum for Burnham's plan to "reindustrialise" Britain.

But he did show his lighter side in a social media video with the prime minister, which saw "Andy and John" bantering about twiglets and scampi fries in the pub. , external

"I will always stand by my political choices as chancellor, including pork scratchings as the best pub snack," he revealed on X.

John Healey: The Basics

Age: 66

Place of birth: Wakefield, West Yorkshire

Education: Lady Lumley's Academy, Pickering; St Peter's School, York; Christ's College, Cambridge

Family: He married Jackie Bate in 1993. The couple have one son, Alex

Constituency: MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, in South Yorkshire

Salary: £166,000

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 5 hours ago

Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor Published 28 September

The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001.

Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.

Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.

He is married and has one son.

He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.

He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.

In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.

He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson , Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."

He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".

And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.

"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.

Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.

Pundits had not touted Healey (right, dressed in a suit) as a frontrunner for the chancellor job

When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.

Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.

At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".

Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families , with a £9bn spending plan.

Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.

In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin , in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.

"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."

Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.

Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

He is not expected to do that in his first Budget, with key spending decisions set to be unveiled next year.

But the tax and spending decisions he does announce on 28 October will still have a huge impact on the success or failure of the fledgling Burnham administration.

stories.summary: The aunt of Zara Aleena says the new powers for judges will "rebalance the power" from offender to victim.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Zara Aleena, a 35-year-old law graduate, was sexually assaulted and murdered by Jordan McSweeney in June 2022

Published 22 October 2026

Tougher punishments for offenders who refuse to attend their sentencings will "rebalance the power" in the justice system, the aunt of murder victim Zara Aleena has said.

From next year, prisoners could be blocked from prison visits and confined to their cells for weeks on end if they do not follow orders to go to court.

This builds on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years.

"A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender. But taking away these privileges would," Farah Naz said.

Naz said the refusal of the man who murdered her niece to go to his sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".

Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.

McSweeney remained in his cell when he was sentenced to life in prison at the Old Bailey later that year.

He was jailed for at least 38 years, which was later reduced to 33 years after he won a Court of Appeal challenge .

Naz said Zara's Aleena's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused".

She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim."

Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.

But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, while social visits could be banned for 27 days and other prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.

For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.

But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".

The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa joined Zara Aleena's family in campaigning for changes to the laws.

All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.

Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.

Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, said the announcement followed "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".

She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

stories.title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
stories.summary: He came to Security Service's attention in the 1930s when he was considered a left-wing firebrand.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Papers show Aneurin Bevan first came to the attention of the security service in the 1930s

Published 22 October 2026

NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files.

Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the Security Service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists.

Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors.

At one stage the-then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him.

But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open.

After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame".

The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933.

One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934.

"Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said.

In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities.

In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists".

Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all.

One MI5 director general was so worried about Bevan's links to a Russian spy he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee (left) about it

"I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943.

"In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently."

The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government.

In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.

Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt.

That May the Security Service's chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him.

One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy.

The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding.

"The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said.

The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died.

stories.body:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say

Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .

Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.

In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.

Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.

The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.

A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.

The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.

K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.

On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.

In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.

In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.

Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”

Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.

The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.

In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”

In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.

“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

stories.body:
When thousands of dying crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups

It was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.

It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.

Environmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.

The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.

In All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”

To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.

Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like the Horizon Post Office scandal , it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.

In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.

They include Seahorse (2019) , following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.

But it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.

We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.

He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”

It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”

Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.

“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”

He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.

Another key figure, snippets of whom we see interspersed throughout, is the Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen, now the Conservative Lord Houchen. He led the concerningly fast demolition of the old steelworks – featuring the largest UK explosion in 75 years – and rapid construction of the Teesside Freeport project in its place.

His denials, as evidence grows that this work may be what caused the die-offs, are a constant frustration for Rennie and the gang. Many of them believe he was involved in corruption and a cover-up, while Houchen denies this, labelling the fishers “activists” and refusing contact with them.

“You can say it’s done,” says Finlay. “It’s not done for Stan. It’s not done for Sue. It’s not done for the scientists … or for Simon Gibbon, the chemist who’s trying to get the dredge licence put on hold.”

That is something the viewers have understood better than the authorities, as money has poured into an NEFC £100,000 fundraiser for the next round of scientific testing. “Someone in Glasgow donated £1,000 during the Q&A on the night, and people have been putting £5 in the pot, it’s pretty amazing.”

Rennie says audience members have been angry on their behalf, and some have cried. “For strangers who aren’t from the area to have that same reaction, it blows your mind.”

Finlay says: “People are becoming infuriated by elected officials who use their enormous platform, their enormous loudhailer, to tell you stories that are greatly at odds with lived experience. Our lives are dominated by tech bros and platforms and conglomerates and people that shout very loudly. And that can often feel disconnected from real life.”

On top of that, Finlay says, people are simply disgusted by the state of the UK’s waterways. “You can sell off all the utilities in the country, and now we’re living with the consequences of that. You can make as many promises as you like, you can promise as many jobs as you like. But the reality is, the trains aren’t working and there’s poo in the river and everyone’s pissed off with that.”

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in cinemas from 23 October.

stories.body:
The UK still imports 60% of its gas and, even with Jackdaw, its energy supply and resilience problems are not going away

A fter the overdue approval of the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur.

To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high.

Equally, though, the “high-impact” bit matters: we’re talking about having enough supplies to run gas-fired power stations at full pelt if necessary to keep the lights on. You don’t take chances.

In short, 10p a month will be added to bills to cover the cost of paying Interconnector Limited, the Belgian owner of the pipeline, to maintain the compressors needed to shove big volumes of gas to Britain in a hurry if required. Without the arrangement, the company had already warned it would cut capacity, in part because the big pipe was not used much in practice last year.

The first conclusion – the comforting one – is that the deal sounds like decent value for money. As insurance policies go, £1.19 a household a year is not much.

The second, however, is that risks to Britain’s gas security are plainly mounting. The Ofgem document describing the Belgian deal says it was “the only currently available intervention identified that both addresses the immediate security of supply position for winter 2026/27 and provides continuing security of supply benefits over the following four years”. It was Belgium, plus any future deal on the Dutch pipeline, or nothing.

Nor is the Belgian shuffle a cure-all. “The agreement does not remove the need for further measures led by government that are likely to be required to support security of supply and wider gas system resilience over the medium and longer term,” says Ofgem.

The government should take that line as a heavy hint to get a move on. Do we need more gas storage, more LNG terminals, or both? And post-Jackdaw, what’s a realistic appraisal of how much will be sourced from the North Sea?

It is now almost a year since an alarming report from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned of an “emerging risk to gas supply security” in 2030. The government promised to “do whatever it takes” to avert a crunch but one cannot say it has actually done much. An interim response to the Neso report came in August but no timetable was given for choosing what kit or arrangements were needed and by when. The final response isn’t due until next year.

Read the “winter outlook” report from National Gas, published on Friday, and a few points stand out. Yes, it’s good news that, with the help of the Belgian deal, this winter’s outlook is positive. But the company also says that, even as annual consumption drifts down slightly, the peaks for demand remain as high as ever, driven by the role of gas-fired power generation when renewables output is low.

after newsletter promotion

Like Ofgem, National Gas says “continued progress on government plans to reform security of supply arrangements will be vital to address enduring challenges in the years ahead”. It is becoming a theme.

The obvious answer is more gas storage to address Britain’s skimpy current levels. That could mean Centrica’s Rough facility in North Sea (currently due to close next spring), the Bains development led by dCarbonX off the north-west coast of England (which may happen anyway), more on-shore salt caverns or any combination. Or, perhaps, German-style forward-buying deals on LNG.

But something has to happen soon. None of this infrastructure gets built quickly and that 2030 potential crunch is getting closer. Certainly, the government cannot agonise for as long as it did over Jackdaw. Eleventh-hour deals with Belgium are not a permanent fix for Britain’s gas security headache.
